title: Writing foundations
description: Understand the reader, verify sources, and write for a concrete task.

lessons.title: What AI technical writing means
lessons.summary: Understand AI, language models, prompts, context, RAG, and agents before using them in documentation.
objectives: Explain the core AI terms in plain language
Separate generation from verification
Map one safe documentation workflow

concepts.definition: Using AI to support documentation work under a defined evidence and review process.
concepts.explanation: AI can help propose outlines, draft from a source packet, edit phrasing, classify topics, compare versions, and suggest tests. These are different tasks with different risks. A rewrite of verified prose has a different review need from generating an undocumented recovery command. Start with the user task and available evidence, then decide where AI provides useful assistance. The writer remains accountable for scope, meaning, and verification.
concepts.example: Use a model to identify missing prerequisites, then have the product owner resolve the gaps.
concepts.caution: Generated fluency is not evidence of product correctness.

concepts.definition: A model that generates text by predicting tokens from context.
concepts.explanation: An LLM is trained on patterns in data and produces a continuation given an input. Its language ability lets it summarize, transform, and draft, but it does not automatically know the authoritative state of your product. It can combine plausible details into an incorrect answer. Supplying source material helps ground the task, while explicit checks determine whether the resulting claims are actually supported.
concepts.example: A model may write a convincing Relay rate-limit policy even though the fixture specifies no rate limit.
concepts.caution: A confident tone does not indicate verified knowledge.

concepts.definition: The instructions and task information supplied to a model.
concepts.explanation: A prompt specifies the requested action, reader, constraints, and output format. It can include source material and examples. A useful drafting prompt tells the model which facts to use, how to handle unknowns, and what structure to return. Prompts are part of the workflow; they are not a replacement for source governance, authorization, or review. Version prompts when comparing outputs so you can trace behavior to changes.
concepts.example: Ask for a procedure, a claim-to-source map, and an unknowns list using R1 only.
concepts.caution: More detailed instructions can still produce unsupported behavior.

concepts.definition: Context is the input available for a generation; tokens are the units processed by the model.
concepts.explanation: A token is a unit used by the model to represent text or other supported input; it is not always a whole word. The context window limits how much input and output the model can handle in one operation. Context can include instructions, conversation, retrieved passages, and tool results. Select relevant evidence and preserve scope rather than adding every document. Important facts can be hard to use when surrounded by unrelated or contradictory material.
concepts.example: Supply the approved v2 contract and the procedure template; exclude the superseded v1 draft.
concepts.caution: A large context window does not make all included evidence valid.

concepts.definition: Retrieving external evidence and providing it to a model for an answer or draft.
concepts.explanation: RAG separates finding evidence from generating language. A retrieval component selects records or passages relevant to a request, using methods such as keyword search, vector similarity, metadata filters, or graph queries. Context assembly then supplies eligible evidence to the model. Evaluate whether the right source was retrieved separately from whether the answer used it correctly. This distinction helps diagnose wrong-version or unsupported answers.
concepts.example: Retrieve approved Relay v2 reference, then answer a parameter question with its source ID.
concepts.caution: Retrieval can return stale or unauthorized evidence unless controls are enforced.

concepts.definition: A workflow coordinates defined steps; an agent may choose actions or tools within limits.
concepts.explanation: A fixed drafting workflow may always retrieve, draft, validate, and request review. An agent may decide which approved search or editing tool to use based on the task. Greater autonomy requires explicit permissions, tool boundaries, state handling, and evaluation. Begin with a controlled workflow when the sequence is known, then add decision-making only when it solves a real need. In this course, exercises are browser-based and do not invoke a live model or autonomous agent.
concepts.example: A controlled helper finds an existing topic before proposing a new draft.
concepts.caution: Do not grant publishing authority just because the system can call a publishing tool.

body: AI-assisted technical writing is a documentation practice with additional tools, rather than automatic product expertise. The durable work is still understanding the reader, obtaining evidence, organizing knowledge, and validating the result. The model can accelerate some steps, but the system around it determines which sources it uses and what reaches the reader.

The course follows a simple chain: understand the task, select authoritative sources, reuse or draft, check support and structure, obtain required review, publish, and maintain. Start with a bounded task such as rewriting one approved procedure. Measure correction effort and failures before expanding to more consequential work.
workflow: Write a prompt with a defined evidence boundary.
Generate or manually draft the topic.
Validate facts, structure, and task usability.
Capture corrections and update the source or process.

annotated.code:
Reader task → Eligible source → Prompt + context → Draft
Draft → Claim verification → User walkthrough → Approval
Failure → Correction → Source, retrieval, prompt, or template update
notes: Source selection precedes generation.
Review determines acceptance; the model does not approve itself.
This is a conceptual workflow, not a live AI service.

exercise.hint: A correct prompt cannot make an obsolete source current.
exercise.solution: Inspect source lifecycle, metadata, and retrieval eligibility. Exclude the obsolete guide, retrieve the approved applicable source, and rerun the answer test. Then check generation support separately.

example.content: A writer supplies an approved procedure and asks for clearer wording. They compare the rewritten steps, warnings, prerequisites, and results against the original before accepting it.

lessons.title: Define the reader and the task
lessons.summary: Write a documentation brief that specifies what a reader must accomplish.
objectives: Write a documentation brief that specifies what a reader must accomplish.
Apply the method to the Relay API course project
Produce and review the specified lab artifact

concepts.definition: The reader’s role, knowledge, and environment.
concepts.explanation: A reader brings prior knowledge, available permissions, a working environment, and a reason for being on the page. Two engineers may need entirely different guidance: one is evaluating an API, while the other is repairing a failed production integration. The useful distinction is what each person already knows and what each can do. A beginner needs a controlled example and explanation of unfamiliar terms; an experienced user needs precise prerequisites, options, and failure paths. Write these assumptions explicitly so reviewers can challenge them.
concepts.example: Brief: an integrator submits a job and checks its result in a sandbox. Success means a valid request, a stored job ID, and correct handling of queued, running, succeeded, and failed states. Production deployment is outside the first quickstart.
concepts.caution: An audience persona full of demographic detail rarely tells you which API steps to include. Replace “Alex is a busy developer who values efficiency” with knowledge, access, environment, and task constraints.

concepts.definition: An observable result that documentation helps the reader reach.
concepts.explanation: Start by recording the reader’s starting state. For Relay, the integrator already understands HTTP and JSON but has not submitted a job. They have access to a sandbox token and a local HTTP client. The documentation should bridge that starting state to an accepted job and a checked result. If token acquisition is undocumented, the quickstart has a prerequisite gap even when its commands are correct.
concepts.example: Brief: an integrator submits a job and checks its result in a sandbox. Success means a valid request, a stored job ID, and correct handling of queued, running, succeeded, and failed states. Production deployment is outside the first quickstart.
concepts.caution: An audience persona full of demographic detail rarely tells you which API steps to include. Replace “Alex is a busy developer who values efficiency” with knowledge, access, environment, and task constraints.

body: A document succeeds when the intended reader can complete a task or make a decision. Start with the action, starting knowledge, environment, constraints, and observable result. “For developers” is too broad: a developer integrating a webhook needs different information from an administrator rotating credentials.

AI can suggest audience questions, but it cannot establish actual user needs without evidence. Use support tickets, interviews, search logs, and observed task failures. Label assumptions so reviewers can distinguish them from findings.

The course uses Relay, a fictional asynchronous job API. Its specification is a teaching fixture, not a real service. The target learner is an experienced writer or an engineer comfortable reading JSON. Beginners can first use Google Technical Writing One. Plan roughly 12–18 hours including labs; actual effort depends on experience.
workflow: Name one user and one task.
Define the expected result and failure conditions.
Write scope, non-goals, and success criteria.

lessons.title: Choose the documentation type
lessons.summary: Separate learning, task guidance, reference, and explanation.
objectives: Separate learning, task guidance, reference, and explanation.
Apply the method to the Relay API course project
Produce and review the specified lab artifact

concepts.definition: A guided learning experience.
concepts.explanation: A documentation type is a promise about the user need the page will satisfy. A tutorial promises a learning experience; a how-to promises a route to a practical outcome; reference promises precise lookup; explanation promises understanding. These promises create different inclusion rules. A tutorial may choose a simple fixed example to teach a concept. Reference must expose all documented constraints without hiding them behind a narrative. An explanation can discuss design rationale that would interrupt a short procedure.
concepts.example: The first-job tutorial contains a runnable sequence. The job-state reference defines legal states. A separate explanation describes why processing is asynchronous.
concepts.caution: Do not put an entire authentication essay between two submission steps. Link to the explanation and keep the procedure focused. Conversely, do not make reference readers follow a tutorial to find whether a field is required.

concepts.definition: Precise descriptions intended for lookup.
concepts.explanation: For Relay, a reader asking “What does queued mean?” needs a state reference or explanation. A reader asking “How do I submit my first job?” needs a tutorial. A reader asking “How do I inspect an existing job?” needs a focused how-to. The same facts can appear in several experiences, but maintain their source once and adapt the presentation deliberately. Cross-links let a reader change needs without forcing every page to become a miniature manual.
concepts.example: The first-job tutorial contains a runnable sequence. The job-state reference defines legal states. A separate explanation describes why processing is asynchronous.
concepts.caution: Do not put an entire authentication essay between two submission steps. Link to the explanation and keep the procedure focused. Conversely, do not make reference readers follow a tutorial to find whether a field is required.

body: Diátaxis distinguishes tutorials, how-to guides, reference, and explanation according to user needs. Apply this as a planning lens rather than forcing every organization into the same menu labels.

A tutorial teaches through a controlled learning experience. A how-to guide solves a task for a reader with relevant knowledge. Reference describes exact behavior. Explanation develops understanding. A quickstart may teach one small task, while detailed parameter constraints belong in reference.

Mixing these needs makes pages harder to use and AI transformations less predictable. Model the type before asking a model to draft. Link to deeper material rather than interrupting a short procedure with an essay.

Check whether the page can meet its purpose without unrelated sections.

lessons.title: Verify facts and edit for clarity
lessons.summary: Establish technical accuracy before polishing language.
objectives: Establish technical accuracy before polishing language.

concepts.definition: The origin and history of a claim.
concepts.explanation: Technical accuracy asks whether the content describes the product correctly. Clarity asks whether the reader can understand and act on that description. A sentence can be accurate but difficult to use, or clear but false. Review these dimensions separately so an editor’s fluency does not substitute for engineering validation. Trace material claims to a contract, tested behavior, or an accountable product decision. Where sources disagree, keep the conflict visible until the authority question is resolved.
concepts.example: Before: “Jobs finish instantly.” Evidence: job submission returns HTTP 202 and a queued state. After: “Submission creates a queued job. Check the job endpoint for processing status.”
concepts.caution: Avoid vague modifiers such as simple, seamless, automatic, and instant unless the evidence supports the precise behavior they imply. “Automatically accepted” can hide authentication and validation conditions.

concepts.definition: Validation of behavior, constraints, and examples.
concepts.explanation: The claim ledger is a small control mechanism. It associates an assertion with its source and applicable context. You do not need to footnote every ordinary word, but endpoint paths, required fields, states, warnings, defaults, and guarantees need evidence. During editing, preserve these invariants. Changing “accepted” to “completed” in a response description changes behavior rather than style.
concepts.example: Before: “Jobs finish instantly.” Evidence: job submission returns HTTP 202 and a queued state. After: “Submission creates a queued job. Check the job endpoint for processing status.”
concepts.caution: Avoid vague modifiers such as simple, seamless, automatic, and instant unless the evidence supports the precise behavior they imply. “Automatically accepted” can hide authentication and validation conditions.

body: Create a fact ledger before drafting: claim, source ID, source version, exact supporting location, reviewer, and unresolved question. Prefer authoritative product specifications and tested behavior over fluent summaries.

Write direct instructions with explicit objects and results. Replace “Simply configure the system appropriately” with the exact setting and its purpose. Define terms, use consistent names, and keep a prerequisite before the step that depends on it.

Editorial review and technical validation are different. A grammatically excellent request example may still use an invalid field. Ask an engineer to resolve product ambiguities; ask an editor to improve readability without changing behavior.
workflow: Have separate technical and editorial reviews.

title: Structured content and metadata

lessons.title: Model reusable content
lessons.summary: Define content fields and relationships that support reuse.
objectives: Define content fields and relationships that support reuse.
Apply the method to the Relay API course project
Produce and review the specified lab artifact

concepts.definition: Types, fields, relationships, and validation rules.
concepts.explanation: A content model names the information types the organization maintains and defines fields, relationships, and rules for each. For a procedure, purpose, prerequisites, actions, expected results, and recovery have distinct meanings. For reference, name, type, requiredness, allowed values, and description matter. The model allows validation to ask meaningful questions: does this procedure explain its result, and does this parameter have a type? A visual heading hierarchy alone cannot answer these reliably.
concepts.example: Procedure model: ID, title, purpose, prerequisites, steps, expected result, recovery, version, source IDs. A missing expected result fails review even if the prose reads well.
concepts.caution: Over-structuring creates form-filling overhead and encourages meaningless placeholder text. Under-structuring hides important context in prose. Test the model on representative procedures, exceptions, and references before standardizing it.

concepts.definition: Using an owned knowledge unit in multiple contexts.
concepts.explanation: Begin with a small model grounded in real topics. Mark a field required only when a missing value creates a material problem. Permit “not applicable” when justified, but do not treat a blank field as approval. Reuse a fragment when its meaning and applicability are stable across contexts; reference it by an identifier so a change can reach dependent topics. Choose Markdown, DITA, or a CMS after modeling the required behavior, not before.
concepts.example: Procedure model: ID, title, purpose, prerequisites, steps, expected result, recovery, version, source IDs. A missing expected result fails review even if the prose reads well.
concepts.caution: Over-structuring creates form-filling overhead and encourages meaningless placeholder text. Under-structuring hides important context in prose. Test the model on representative procedures, exceptions, and references before standardizing it.

body: Structured content gives information a predictable semantic shape. A procedure can require purpose, prerequisites, numbered steps, expected result, recovery guidance, and applicable version. A concept and an API reference need different fields.

Formatting alone is insufficient. Bold text does not tell a system whether it is a warning, prerequisite, or parameter. Markdown plus a validated template and front matter can be enough for a small team. DITA or a component CMS may suit larger reuse, localization, and variant requirements; choose from actual workflow needs.

Reuse the source knowledge while preserving context. A warning about rotating a production credential cannot be detached from its consequence and placed indiscriminately in every guide. Give reusable fragments stable identifiers, scope, owners, and change dependencies.
workflow: Define reusable fragments and stable IDs.

lessons.title: Design useful metadata
lessons.summary: Use metadata to determine applicability, trust, and lifecycle.
objectives: Use metadata to determine applicability, trust, and lifecycle.
Apply the method to the Relay API course project
Produce and review the specified lab artifact

concepts.definition: A governed classification vocabulary.
concepts.explanation: Content structure describes what a topic contains. Metadata describes where it applies and how it may be used. A procedure can be structurally complete yet unsuitable because it is for v1, still in draft, or restricted to incident responders. Retrieval needs both relevance and eligibility. Relevance is how well information matches a task; eligibility is whether the system is allowed to use that information in this context. A highly relevant document can still be ineligible.
concepts.example: A v1 draft and an approved v2 guide mention the same endpoint. Filtering by product=Relay, version=2, status=approved, and permitted access excludes the draft.
concepts.caution: An access label is not access enforcement. A trusted application must authorize the user and exclude unauthorized records before model context assembly. Also, “last reviewed yesterday” does not imply that a page applies to the current product version.

concepts.definition: Attributes describing applicability, authority, and use.
concepts.explanation: Design metadata backward from decisions. If the assistant must answer only for v2, version becomes a required filterable attribute. If only reviewed guidance is eligible, approval status needs a controlled vocabulary and an authoritative review transition. If ownership drives corrections, owner must resolve to a team that accepts the work. Record unknown values explicitly and define whether they block the use case. Propagate required context to chunks, exports, and transformed assets.
concepts.example: A v1 draft and an approved v2 guide mention the same endpoint. Filtering by product=Relay, version=2, status=approved, and permitted access excludes the draft.
concepts.caution: An access label is not access enforcement. A trusted application must authorize the user and exclude unauthorized records before model context assembly. Also, “last reviewed yesterday” does not imply that a page applies to the current product version.

body: Metadata describes content so people and systems can select and manage it. Start with fields that enable real decisions: topic ID, content type, audience, product, version, owner, status, source IDs, last reviewed date, and access classification. Add effective dates, locale, and review triggers where the use case requires them.

Use controlled values, stable IDs, validation, and field owners. An AI classifier may propose tags; a responsible person confirms ambiguous labels. Avoid collecting dozens of fields that nobody maintains. Missing or unknown metadata should be handled explicitly rather than silently defaulted to approved.

Metadata does not enforce access by itself. Retrieval must apply authenticated permission checks on the server before context reaches the model. A public/internal label in front matter is an input to policy, not a security boundary. Propagate source identity and applicability to each indexed chunk.
workflow: Write the decisions each field supports.
Define controlled values and required fields.
Set handling for unknown or expired values.
Verify metadata survives export and indexing.

lessons.title: Manage versions and dependencies
lessons.summary: Preserve context when content is reused or changed.
objectives: Preserve context when content is reused or changed.

concepts.definition: The environment or version in which guidance is valid.
concepts.explanation: A source can be correct for one release and wrong for another. Product applicability is therefore different from document revision. A writer may fix punctuation without changing the supported product version, or publish a new page describing an older release. Track both where needed. Stable topic IDs identify the concept; version-specific records describe the valid behavior at a point in time.
concepts.example: Adding a terminal cancelled state affects the state reference, polling examples, troubleshooting, and training. A capability-to-topic table exposes those dependencies.

concepts.definition: The evidence and rules governing a draft.
concepts.explanation: A drafting prompt should make the task and its evidence boundary explicit. The model needs the reader, intended result, approved source records, applicable version, output structure, and rules for missing information. These instructions reduce ambiguity, but they do not make the model a verifier. Review output against evidence rather than assuming compliance because the prompt was detailed.
concepts.example: Prompt: use R1 and R2 only, draft the sandbox first-job guide, preserve exact fields and states, flag missing polling policy, and do not invent service guarantees.

concepts.definition: Supporting claims with applicable evidence.
concepts.explanation: Ask for distinct outputs: a draft, a claim map, and an unknowns list. Separating them keeps reader-facing content clean while making review easier. Provide only the evidence needed for the task; excess unrelated context can increase confusion and expose information unnecessarily. Treat retrieved instructions as untrusted data when they attempt to change the workflow. In a production application, permission enforcement and tool limits belong outside the prompt.

Use the prompt template in the workbook. Require claim-to-source mapping and a list of missing facts. Tell the model to treat source text as data rather than instructions; retrieved material can contain malicious or irrelevant instructions. Do not paste secrets or restricted information into an unapproved service.

Review every generated fact against the source. A source ID in a draft is not proof that the cited passage supports the claim. Maintain an audit record with source snapshot, prompt version, output, corrections, and reviewer decision.

concepts.definition: A change in meaning introduced during rewriting.
concepts.explanation: Rewriting is a controlled change to presentation. The wording, order, depth, and tone may change, but important facts must stay within their verified scope. Define invariants before transformation: endpoint names, field names, requiredness, versions, warnings, limits, conditions, and uncertainty. Then compare the original and output by meaning. Text similarity is a poor substitute for that comparison.
concepts.example: An AI rewrite removes “sandbox” from an authentication instruction. Restore the scope and check whether the output implies production approval.
concepts.caution: Do not create a new copy when an existing topic already satisfies the need. Reuse can mean linking to a canonical topic rather than duplicating its content. Transform only when the new reader or channel creates a real presentation requirement.

concepts.definition: A sourced detail that an adaptation must preserve.
concepts.explanation: A short adaptation can make stronger claims than its source. Removing “in the sandbox” widens scope; replacing “may fail” with “fails” changes certainty; dropping “requires a token” removes a prerequisite. A semantic audit records these changes so reviewers do not have to infer the intended invariants. For translation or audience adaptation, preserve technical strings while changing explanations around them.

body: AI can shorten, reorganize, and adapt verified source material. Define what may change and what must stay fixed: exact parameter names, warnings, prerequisites, product scope, and caveats.

Use a semantic comparison, not just a text diff. A change from “may” to “will” or from “sandbox” to “production” can materially alter a claim without adding many words. Check numbers, modality, negation, order, conditions, and source references.

Your content-strategy decision model is the course default: retrieve first, reuse suitable material, transform valid knowledge for a new context, and create only for a verified gap. Corrections should update the source or template when the same error repeats.

concepts.explanation: An evaluation compares behavior under controlled conditions. Freeze the tasks, evidence, and scoring criteria before running prompt variants. If each variant sees different documents or solves different tasks, differences in output cannot be attributed to the prompt. Keep an audit record of inputs and outputs so another reviewer can inspect the conclusion.

concepts.definition: A decision including control, cost, and ongoing maintenance.
concepts.explanation: Measure correction effort as well as first-pass scores. A draft may have one small but dangerous error and require more review than a less polished draft with visible unknowns. Track unsupported claims, missing prerequisites, structural compliance, and reviewer time. Use several task types and boundary cases, then label the experiment’s limits. More elaborate prompting can hide a broken source process. Investigate whether failures come from source gaps, retrieval, instructions, or generation. Pick a lightweight setup when it meets requirements; build integrations when repeat volume and control needs justify maintenance.

concepts.definition: A short path to one useful first result.
concepts.explanation: A quickstart selects a narrow path through a product so a reader can experience one useful result. It should minimize optional choices, explain prerequisites before they are needed, and show the output after each important step. A good quickstart does not claim to be complete reference. It links readers to deeper material once they have enough context to use it.
concepts.example: The quickstart includes a sandbox placeholder URL clearly marked as fictional. It asks the reader to store job_id and inspect the final state rather than promising immediate completion.
concepts.caution: A command that parses correctly is not necessarily usable. Fresh-reader testing exposes missing setup, ambiguous placeholders, unexpected outputs, and hidden permissions. For Relay, a walkthrough is a contract simulation unless an approved live service is provided.

concepts.definition: The observable output after a step.
concepts.explanation: For an asynchronous API, success is not one event. Authentication must be valid, submission must be accepted, the returned ID must be retained, and later state must be interpreted. Write the guide around these transitions. Distinguish an example response from an actual observed response, especially when teaching with mocks. A reader should know exactly which parts are executable and which are illustrative.

body: A quickstart should minimize choices while retaining the prerequisites needed for success. Explain the sandbox requirement, token scope, expected HTTP status, and how to inspect the result. Link to detailed reference for optional parameters.

concepts.definition: A specification of interface behavior.
concepts.explanation: API reference represents the interface precisely enough for a reader to construct valid requests and interpret responses. It needs method, path, authentication, media type, parameters, request body, response shape, status codes, and documented constraints. A machine-readable contract can generate much of this skeleton. Descriptions and examples supply meaning that a schema alone may not capture.

concepts.definition: Checking values against types and constraints.
concepts.explanation: Validate both the contract and the resulting documentation. A generator can be internally consistent while exposing an outdated or incorrect schema. Compare requiredness, field types, enum values, path parameters, and sample outputs. Preserve unknowns as product questions until authoritative evidence resolves them. Do not infer retry semantics or idempotency from HTTP status alone.
concepts.example: A generated table calls source_url optional. The specification says required. Correct the table and add a schema validation check so the error cannot recur silently.

body: An API reference should cover method, path, authentication, request fields, validation, responses, error behavior, and examples. Use an OpenAPI contract when available, but reconcile it with implementation tests and product decisions; generated reference can faithfully reproduce a wrong contract.

Separate documented behavior from unknowns. The Relay fixture defines 400 for a missing source_url, 401 for an invalid token, and 404 for an unknown job ID. It does not specify rate limits, idempotency, retry timing, or production retention. These remain product questions.

AI can draft descriptions from a schema, but review field names, requiredness, types, enums, and examples mechanically where possible. Add explanatory examples for ambiguous behavior rather than allowing the model to guess defaults.

concepts.definition: Evidence-led diagnosis and recovery.
concepts.explanation: Troubleshooting starts from what the reader observes, not from an assumed root cause. Organize a path from symptom to diagnostic evidence, likely causes, corrective action, verification, and escalation. A single symptom may have several causes. State the evidence that distinguishes them rather than presenting a universal fix. Safe troubleshooting avoids commands that bypass controls or destroy useful state without authorization.
concepts.example: A 401 means the request lacks valid authentication under the fixture. Check the token configuration without exposing the token. Do not recommend bypassing authorization.
concepts.caution: A proposed teaching change is not a released capability. In exercises, label new states or endpoints hypothetical and update the contract before treating them as valid in a new version.

concepts.definition: A verified description of change and user impact.
concepts.explanation: Release notes solve a different problem: what changed, who is affected, and what action is needed. Classify changes and preserve version scope. A changelog assembled from commits needs product review because internal implementation activity may not represent external behavior. Link to migration guidance when a change breaks existing use.
concepts.example: A 401 means the request lacks valid authentication under the fixture. Check the token configuration without exposing the token. Do not recommend bypassing authorization.

body: Troubleshooting should connect an observed symptom to a verified cause, diagnostic check, and recovery path. Avoid confidently naming a root cause when a symptom has several explanations. Explain when to stop and escalate.

Release notes connect a verified change to user impact and action. Distinguish added, changed, fixed, deprecated, and removed behavior. Preserve affected version and migration requirements. A commit message alone may not describe customer impact.

AI can cluster incident reports or draft change summaries, but support and engineering should verify causes and remediation. Treat logs as potentially sensitive, redact secrets, and validate that commands are appropriate for the user’s environment.

concepts.definition: A retrievable unit with enough context and identifiers.
concepts.explanation: A chunk is the unit the retrieval system can return. Its size and boundaries determine which context travels together. Fixed-size splitting is simple and repeatable, but can cut a procedure before its expected result or detach a warning from its action. Topic-aware splitting tries to keep meaningful units intact. Neither strategy is universally best; compare retrieval behavior for representative questions and constraints.
concepts.example: Query: “How do I check a Relay v2 job?” Correct context contains GET /v2/jobs/{job_id}, states, and the applicable version. A similar v1 draft is ineligible even if its wording matches better.
concepts.caution: Embeddings encode similarity, not permission or truth. Even good semantic matches can be stale or ineligible. Apply trusted filters and ranking policy, then verify whether the selected evidence supports the requested task.

concepts.definition: Retrieving external evidence for model generation.
concepts.explanation: A chunk should retain identity, heading path, parent topic, product version, eligibility context, and source location. Smaller chunks can improve focus but require recovering parent context. Larger chunks can preserve context but include irrelevant details. Query type matters: a parameter lookup needs a small precise passage, while a multi-step recovery path may require a complete procedure. Test the context assembled for generation, not only which snippets ranked first.
concepts.example: Query: “How do I check a Relay v2 job?” Correct context contains GET /v2/jobs/{job_id}, states, and the applicable version. A similar v1 draft is ineligible even if its wording matches better.
concepts.caution: Embeddings encode similarity, not permission or truth. Even good semantic matches can be stale or ineligible. Apply trusted filters and ranking policy, then verify whether the selected evidence supports the requested task.

body: Chunk content around coherent units such as a complete procedure or a section that answers one question. Fixed-size splitting is a useful baseline, but it can separate a warning from its step or a parameter description from its heading. Compare alternatives with representative queries.

Attach topic ID, chunk ID, heading path, product version, audience, approval status, source location, and authorization information where supported. Use server-enforced filters before generation. Preserve parent links to recover wider context when a snippet is incomplete.

Good structure and metadata improve the available signals; they do not guarantee retrieval accuracy. Test lexical and semantic retrieval, ranking, permissions, and source freshness separately. A graph is useful for relationship questions and dependency traversal; it is not required for every documentation assistant.
workflow: Compare results on the same query set.

concepts.definition: Versioned cases with expected evidence and behavior.
concepts.explanation: An evaluation case pairs an input with expected evidence and acceptable behavior. It is more than a list of questions. Without a reference source and rubric, a reviewer may reward a plausible answer that is unsupported. Version the cases as product behavior changes, and record why each case exists. Include common tasks and cases that expose specific risks.
concepts.example: Case: “What is Relay’s guaranteed completion time?” Expected response: the fixture specifies no guarantee; do not invent one. A confident duration fails even if the answer sounds useful.
concepts.caution: A model judge can help score a large set but is another system needing calibration. Compare its judgments with expert labels, inspect disagreement patterns, and keep critical factual or access failures under explicit human review.

concepts.definition: Whether evidence supports a specific claim.
concepts.explanation: Separate retrieval evaluation from answer evaluation. First ask whether the eligible supporting source was selected and ineligible evidence excluded. Then ask whether the response uses that source correctly, preserves constraints, and helps the user act. This separation reveals whether a correction belongs in content, indexing, retrieval, prompt design, or generation. An answer can be accidentally correct despite failed retrieval.
concepts.example: Case: “What is Relay’s guaranteed completion time?” Expected response: the fixture specifies no guarantee; do not invent one. A confident duration fails even if the answer sounds useful.
concepts.caution: A model judge can help score a large set but is another system needing calibration. Compare its judgments with expert labels, inspect disagreement patterns, and keep critical factual or access failures under explicit human review.

body: Create cases from actual user tasks and known failure modes. Each record contains question, user/context, eligible evidence, expected behavior, prohibited behavior, and scoring rubric. Include wrong-version, no-answer, incomplete-source, restricted-source, and misleading-source cases.

Measure retrieval success separately from answer quality. A correct answer from model memory can hide retrieval failure. Check whether the expected eligible evidence is present, then whether every material claim is supported and whether the reader can act on the response.

A model judge can help triage outputs, but it must be calibrated against expert labels. Record disagreements and evaluate sensitive cases with humans. Fluent wording and AI-detector scores do not establish technical accuracy or authorship.

concepts.definition: A defined check that controls progression.
concepts.explanation: A gate is a check that determines whether work proceeds, is corrected, or escalates. Define input, criterion, evidence, owner, and failure action. “Review quality” is too vague. “The technical reviewer confirms every endpoint example against approved v2 evidence, and unsupported interface claims block publication” is actionable. Put checks where they prevent the most rework.
concepts.example: A draft is readable but omits authentication and includes an invented production URL. Block publication, repair the evidence and prerequisites, then rerun the walkthrough.
concepts.caution: An average score can hide a blocking defect. A document with excellent tone, layout, and accessibility still fails if its command is wrong or it exposes unauthorized information. Define critical failures independently of weighted rubric scores.

concepts.definition: Matching review depth to the consequence of error.
concepts.explanation: Use deterministic automation where the rule is explicit: required fields, schema validity, stale dates, broken links, prohibited terminology, and example syntax. Human review handles ambiguity, user experience, technical judgment, and unresolved risk. Record exceptions as decisions with an owner and revisit trigger; otherwise they become silent policy drift.
concepts.example: A draft is readable but omits authentication and includes an invented production URL. Block publication, repair the evidence and prerequisites, then rerun the walkthrough.
concepts.caution: An average score can hide a blocking defect. A document with excellent tone, layout, and accessibility still fails if its command is wrong or it exposes unauthorized information. Define critical failures independently of weighted rubric scores.

body: Use gates at request, retrieval, draft, risk review, approval, and publication. A required-field check belongs before editorial review; a product ambiguity belongs with engineering. Give each gate an owner, evidence, and pass/fail condition.

Automate checks with reliable definitions: schema validation, broken links, approved terminology, code syntax, missing metadata, and expired review dates. Use human review for factual ambiguity, usability, complex risk, and changes to product meaning.

The course quality rubric covers accuracy, source support, completeness, task usability, accessibility, and maintainability. A release fails on any unsupported critical claim or unauthorized source disclosure regardless of its average score. Track repeated corrections back to the responsible system layer.

concepts.definition: Applying software change practices to documentation.
concepts.explanation: Docs-as-code borrows practices from software development: versioned source, focused branches, reviewable diffs, repeatable builds, and automated checks. Its value is the controlled workflow, not the Markdown extension. A documentation change can be traced to a product change and reviewed with the same care as an interface change. Teams may still use a CMS if equivalent controls meet their needs.
concepts.example: Repository layout: docs/, specifications/, examples/, evaluation/, and review/. A pull request changes the source contract and every dependent example in one reviewable release.
concepts.caution: A successful build proves only what the build checks. It does not prove every command works or every claim is correct. Keep source, rendering, technical validation, and user walkthrough evidence distinct.

concepts.definition: A specific version prepared for approval and publishing.
concepts.explanation: A useful review description explains behavior before and after, the evidence used, affected assets, validation performed, and unresolved questions. Build the exact candidate that will be released so reviewers see its rendered behavior. Generated files should have a reproducible source; otherwise a manual fix may disappear at the next build. Coordinate documentation releases with product applicability.
concepts.example: Repository layout: docs/, specifications/, examples/, evaluation/, and review/. A pull request changes the source contract and every dependent example in one reviewable release.
concepts.caution: A successful build proves only what the build checks. It does not prove every command works or every claim is correct. Keep source, rendering, technical validation, and user walkthrough evidence distinct.

body: Docs-as-code stores documentation source alongside version control, review, build, and deployment practices. It can support Markdown, schemas, generated reference, and automated checks without requiring a particular platform.

Use a branch, a meaningful diff, and a review request that identifies product behavior, evidence, tests, and remaining questions. Build previews before publication. Run link, schema, and example checks against the version being released.

Do not place credentials in sample source or build logs. Use clearly marked placeholders and an approved secret-handling mechanism. Keep rollout and rollback procedures documented so a content defect can be corrected quickly.

objectives: Maintain owners, review triggers, and measurable feedback.

Produce and review the specified lab artifact

concepts.definition: Creation, approval, maintenance, and retirement.
concepts.explanation: Documentation can become incorrect without anyone editing it. Product behavior changes, sources expire, owners move teams, and user tasks evolve. Lifecycle management defines how those events trigger review and how invalid content is retired or preserved for historical use. A review date is a reminder, not a guarantee of current validity.
concepts.example: A release changes authentication. Trigger source, quickstart, and troubleshooting reviews immediately rather than waiting for the quarterly review date.
concepts.caution: Page traffic measures exposure, not success. A popular troubleshooting page can indicate either useful guidance or a recurring product defect. Combine quantitative signals with observed task outcomes and evidence about what users actually did.

concepts.definition: Returning observed failures to source and process owners.
concepts.explanation: Assign accountability to a durable team when possible. The topic owner maintains the user experience; the source owner resolves factual questions; the approver controls release. Small teams may combine these roles, but still make the decisions explicit. Feedback should produce a correction at the responsible layer: content, metadata, source authority, retrieval, or workflow.
concepts.example: A release changes authentication. Trigger source, quickstart, and troubleshooting reviews immediately rather than waiting for the quarterly review date.
concepts.caution: Page traffic measures exposure, not success. A popular troubleshooting page can indicate either useful guidance or a recurring product defect. Combine quantitative signals with observed task outcomes and evidence about what users actually did.

body: Ownership must survive organizational change. Assign topic and source owners, review triggers, and retirement criteria. Review dates are useful reminders, but product changes and user failures should trigger review sooner.

Use feedback to improve the system. A recurring wrong-version answer may require indexing rules; repeated terminology edits may require a vocabulary update; a failing task may require better prerequisites or a product fix.

Measure task completion, issue recurrence, support deflection where measurable, source freshness, reuse, review effort, and critical defects. Establish a baseline and document sampling limitations. Do not claim business impact from page views alone.
workflow: Review outcomes and retire unused or invalid topics.

lessons.summary: Demonstrate a trusted AI-assisted documentation workflow.
objectives: Demonstrate a trusted AI-assisted documentation workflow.

concepts.definition: An integrated demonstration of applied skills.
concepts.explanation: A capstone is an integrated artifact plus evidence of how it was produced and checked. The final documentation pages are only part of the result. Include the brief, source ledger, content model, metadata, drafts, corrections, evaluation set, review record, and maintenance plan. These show whether the learner can make defensible decisions rather than merely produce polished text.
concepts.example: A portfolio description says: “Designed a fictional Relay API documentation workflow; tested examples against a supplied contract; recorded reviewer corrections.” It does not claim deployment or measured enterprise savings.
concepts.caution: Do not present mock execution, fictional stakeholders, or simulated metrics as production outcomes. A clear limitation strengthens the evidence because it tells a reader exactly what was tested and what remains unverified.

concepts.definition: The boundary of what the evidence actually proves.
concepts.explanation: Use the practical rubric to assess the package separately from the knowledge quiz. Score observable evidence, not confidence or claimed expertise. A reviewer should be able to reproduce a contract check, follow the walkthrough, and inspect why a release decision was made. If a real product is used instead of Relay, obtain permission and sanitize source material before publishing a portfolio case.
concepts.example: A portfolio description says: “Designed a fictional Relay API documentation workflow; tested examples against a supplied contract; recorded reviewer corrections.” It does not claim deployment or measured enterprise savings.
concepts.caution: Do not present mock execution, fictional stakeholders, or simulated metrics as production outcomes. A clear limitation strengthens the evidence because it tells a reader exactly what was tested and what remains unverified.

body: Assemble the documentation system built across the course: reader brief, source ledger, content model, metadata dictionary, four topics, chunk manifest, evaluation cases, and release record. Explain where AI helped and what humans verified.

Capstone scoring is separate from the multiple-choice final assessment. Use 25 points for technical accuracy, 20 for source support, 15 for structure and metadata, 15 for task usability, 15 for evaluation, and 10 for maintenance and release control. Target 80/100 with no critical factual, access, or safety failures.

A self-assessment is learning evidence, not professional certification. Ask a technical reviewer and a fresh reader to examine the work when available. State that the project is fictional and describe verification limits; do not present simulated metrics as customer outcomes.
workflow: Run all validation and evaluation cases.
Write a decision record: release, revise, or hold.
